parsed.hook: Woodruff Vineyard sits high enough in the Santa Cruz Mountains to stay cooler than the valleys below, and that mountain air shows up as a Pinot Noir with red fruit, citrus lift, and a peppery edge. At around $40–$50 on release, this is not a cheap bottle; it is a site-specific California Pinot for people who want tension over plushness.
parsed.wine_summary:
Wind Gap built its reputation on low-intervention wines that put site ahead of makeup, and Woodruff Vineyard is a sharp example of that idea. The 2014 Pinot Noir is described with tiny strawberry, rhubarb, floral notes, and no oak covering the fruit; that points to a wine built for clarity, not sweetness or weight. The Santa Cruz Mountains AVA gives it the raw material: elevated ridges above the marine fog layer, steep slopes, and thin shale, sandstone, and shallow rocky soils that drain fast and force the vine to work. That combination usually gives Pinot Noir a brighter red-fruit profile, firmer line, and more savory detail than you get from richer coastal valley sites.

What makes Wind Gap distinctive is the refusal to sand down those edges. The house style favors freshness, transparency, and food-friendly alcohol levels rather than the sweeter, riper California Pinot register. In this wine, that means the vineyard is doing the talking: less black fruit, less sweet oak spice, more blood orange, herbs, and a cool-climate snap that keeps the palate moving.
parsed.terroir_expression: Santa Cruz Mountains Pinot Noir from a site like Woodruff tastes like elevation plus fog. The AVA’s steep, fractured shale and sandstone soils drain quickly, so berries tend to stay small and concentrated, while the marine layer slows ripening and preserves acidity; that is why the wine reads more as red cherry, citrus peel, and dried herbs than jam. The heavy fog mentioned in the notes likely compresses the midpalate, which is why the wine can feel compact at first and then open into perfume with air.
parsed.vinification_summary: This bottling was done with 100% whole clusters, which means the ferment included intact bunches rather than fully destemmed berries. Whole-cluster fermentation raises aromatic lift and adds tannin from stems, so the wine can smell more floral and peppery while feeling a little more structured and less sugary on the palate. That fits Wind Gap’s approach: minimal oak imprint, light extraction, and a cellar hand that aims to preserve the vineyard’s high-toned fruit and mountain tension rather than thicken it up.
food_pairing: Duck breast with sour cherry sauce: the wine’s red fruit and natural acidity cut the duck’s richness, and the cherry note echoes the sauce without making the pairing taste sweet.
Nashville hot chicken: the wine’s low-oak profile and bright acid handle the spice better than a heavier Pinot, and the stem-driven pepper note plays well with the heat.
Mushroom and taleggio pizza: earthy mushrooms meet the wine’s savory side, while the cheese gets enough lift from the acidity to stay from feeling heavy.
Poulet rôti with thyme and preserved lemon: the herbal notes and citrus edge in the wine lock onto the roast chicken’s skin and the lemon’s salinity.
At a fine-dining table, roasted quail with black trumpet mushrooms and a cherry glaze works because the wine has the restraint and perfume to keep pace without bulldozing the bird.
comparable_wines: Rhys Alpine Vineyard Pinot Noir — another Santa Cruz Mountains Pinot built from elevation, cool air, and mineral drive, with a similarly tensile profile.
Sandhi Sta. Rita Hills Pinot Noir — same commitment to low-oak, site-first Pinot, though with more wind-swept saline and less mountain herbality.
Arnot-Roberts Trout Gulch Pinot Noir — comparable for its lean frame, high-toned fruit, and refusal to pad the middle.
parsed.style_profile: Light-bodied dry Pinot Noir with firm stem-derived structure and lifted red-fruit perfume
parsed.cellar_recommendation: Drink 2014 now through the next several years if the bottle is well stored. Keep it at 55°F, dark, and humid if possible; this style improves with air but will not benefit from long decanting once it passes its peak.
parsed.value_assessment: $40–$50 at release is fair for a single-vineyard Santa Cruz Mountains Pinot from Wind Gap, because the wine is about place-specific character rather than broad commercial polish. At that price, it competes with Rhys Santa Cruz Mountains Pinot Noir and Sandhi Sta. Rita Hills Pinot Noir; I would buy this over either if you want more floral lift and mountain savor, not more sheer fruit volume. It is worth it for people who value site clarity and lower alcohol over richness.
parsed.market_position: This belongs on the shelves and lists that serve Burgundy-minded California drinkers, not casual Pinot buyers looking for sweetness and easy fruit. Restaurants with serious by-the-glass or reserve Pinot programs should use it for duck, mushroom, and game dishes; retailers can place it next to leaner Santa Cruz Mountains and Sta. Rita Hills bottles for customers who know the difference. Collectors who track cult California producers will care too, but the real audience is drinkers who want a Pinot with acid line and a sense of altitude.
parsed.insider_take: The tradeoff is obvious: if you want dark, plush California Pinot, skip this bottle. Woodruff Vineyard is for people who like their Pinot angular at first, then perfumed and quietly persistent after a few minutes in the glass. Most buyers underrate how much whole-cluster fermentation can sharpen a wine’s personality; here it gives the wine its spice, lift, and grip without turning it into a stemmy caricature.
